393.title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6–7)
393.hook: the least in his family asks for signs and wins with 300
393.howItsDone: Catholics hear Gideon's call in the Mass readings, and in traditional Marian devotion the dew-soaked fleece is honored as a figure of Mary and the Incarnation, drawn from the Church Fathers and old Advent hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Deborah under her palm, and a commander who wouldn't go without her. Your line was she judged israel. Whose leadership did you notice? Day three hundred ninety-three.

A young man is threshing wheat in a winepress. That's an odd place for it. You thresh on an open hilltop where the wind can carry the chaff away. But raiders from Midian have been stripping the land every harvest, so he's hiding, beating out a little grain in a pit where nobody will see. And that's where an angel finds him, and sits down under an oak, and greets him with a line that sounds almost like a joke: "The Lord is with thee, O most valiant of men." The most valiant of men is crouched in a hole, hiding his breakfast. His name is Gideon, Gedeon in the Douay-Rheims.
screen: `THRESHING WHEAT IN A WINEPRESS.` → `HIDING FROM THE RAIDERS.` → `O MOST VALIANT OF MEN.`

segments.voice: Gideon doesn't believe it. He says, in the Douay: "Behold my family is the meanest in Manasses, and I am the least in my father's house." The poorest clan, the youngest son. And he wants proof. So he lays a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asks God for dew on the fleece only, with the ground dry. In the morning he wrings out a bowl of water. Then, nervously, he asks for the reverse: dry fleece, wet ground. And God does that too. The text doesn't scold him for asking. Now the army. Gideon gathers thirty-two thousand men, and God says: too many. The reason is blunt: "lest Israel should glory against me, and say: I was delivered by my own strength." Twenty-two thousand go home. Ten thousand left, and still too many. At the water, God sets apart the three hundred who lap. People often say the three hundred were picked for being alert. The text never says that. They're simply fewer. With trumpets, clay jars and torches, three hundred men throw a vast camp into panic in the night. And Catholics have a second way of seeing the fleece. Early Christian writers, Saint Ambrose among them, saw in the dew falling on the fleece alone a figure of the Incarnation, God's gift coming down quietly on one woman, Mary. Even the angel's greeting, the Lord is with thee, rings for Catholics like a first draft of Gabriel's. The thread through it all: God picks the least, and trims the army, so nobody can mistake who won.
screen: `THE LEAST IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE.` · `DEW ON THE FLEECE, THEN DRY.` · `THIRTY-TWO THOUSAND TO THREE HUNDRED.` · `THE FATHERS SAW MARY IN THE DEW.` · then, large: `I WAS DELIVERED BY MY OWN STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust with less than you want. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place where you feel short. Not enough time this week. Not enough money. Not enough people on the project, not enough patience at home. Name it plainly. Then imagine the number going down, the way Gideon's did, and ask what you could still do with what's left. One hour, used well. One friend. One honest try. If you pray, you can hand that small number to God the way Gideon held out his fleece. The bell holds the time.
Gideon's fleece. The sign a frightened judge asked for, twice, and was given. Since then, putting out a fleece means asking God for a sign. Today's word.
Your line: fewer is enough. Today, when you catch yourself thinking you can't start until you have more, start with what's in your hands. Day three hundred ninety-three.

394.title: Samson (Judges 13–16)
394.hook: great strength, poor choices, and one last prayer
394.howItsDone: Catholics hear the announcement of Samson's birth at daily Mass in late Advent, paired with the angel's announcement of John the Baptist's birth, and the Church reads his life as a warning as much as an example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's fleece, and an army cut down to three hundred. Your line was fewer is enough. What did you start with less? Day three hundred ninety-four.

Every December, a few days before Christmas, Catholics at daily Mass hear a story that starts like the Gospel. A woman who has never been able to have children is visited by a messenger of God. You will conceive and bear a son, he tells her, and no razor will touch his head. He'll be set apart for God from his mother's womb. That child grows up to be the strongest man in the Bible. He tears a lion apart with his hands. He carries off a city's gates. And he makes almost every wrong choice a strong man can make. His name is Samson.
screen: `A DECEMBER READING.` → `NO RAZOR SHALL TOUCH HIS HEAD.` → `THE STRONGEST MAN IN THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Samson is a Nazarite, a Nazirite in most English Bibles: someone consecrated to God, who drinks no wine and never cuts his hair. The long hair is the sign of the vow. The strength is God's gift. Keep those two apart, because Samson doesn't. He marries outside his people against his parents' pleading. He sets three hundred foxes loose with torches in the enemy's fields. He's ruled by appetite and revenge, and the text tells it straight, without excuse. Then Delilah. Three times she asks what makes him strong, three times he lies, and three times the Philistines burst in. The fourth time he tells her the truth, in the Douay-Rheims: "if my head be shaven, my strength shall depart from me." She lulls him to sleep, and a barber shaves his seven locks. Here's the line that matters most. He wakes and thinks he'll shake himself free as before, "not knowing that the Lord was departed from him." The hair wasn't magic. It was the last piece of a promise he'd been breaking for years. Blinded and chained, he grinds grain in a prison. His hair starts to grow. At a feast for their god, they bring him out to mock him, and he prays: "O Lord God, remember me, and restore to me now my former strength." He pushes the pillars, and the house falls on him and on them. The Church doesn't hold Samson up as a model of virtue. But the Letter to the Hebrews names him among the people of faith. Strength never made Samson wise. At the end, it was a prayer that made him remember who his strength belonged to.
screen: `A NAZARITE: SET APART FOR GOD.` · `STRONG, AND RULED BY APPETITE.` · `THE LORD WAS DEPARTED FROM HIM.` · `REMEMBER ME, O LORD GOD.` · then, large: `RESTORE TO ME NOW MY FORMER STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your weakness. Settle, and breathe. Samson's trouble wasn't a lack of strength. It was a soft spot he kept walking back into: flattery, anger, wanting what he wanted. Name yours, quietly, to yourself. The thing that gets past your guard every time. Don't argue with it. Just look at it the way you'd look at a door you keep leaving unlocked. If you pray, you can borrow Samson's words: O Lord God, remember me. If you don't, simply let yourself be seen, by yourself, without excuses. The bell holds the time.
Samson. A judge consecrated to God from the womb, given great strength, who ruined much of it, and whose last act was a prayer. Today's word.
Your line: strength isn't wisdom. Today, when you feel most sure of yourself, pause one breath before you act. Day three hundred ninety-four.

395.title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
395.hook: a Moabite widow refuses to leave her mother-in-law: thy people shall be my people
395.howItsDone: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and her promise to Naomi is one of the Old Testament readings couples may choose for a Catholic wedding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson, the strongest man in the book, undone by his own choices and saved at the end by a prayer. Your line was strength isn't wisdom. When did you pause before acting? Day three hundred ninety-five.

Three widows stand on a road. One is old: Naomi, Noemi in the Douay-Rheims. She left Bethlehem in a famine with her husband and two sons, and in the land of Moab she buried all three. The other two are young, Moabite women who married her sons. Now Naomi is walking home with nothing, and she stops and tells them: go back. Go home to your mothers. I have no more sons for you. There's nothing for you where I'm going. They cry. One of them, Orpah, kisses her and turns back, and nobody in the story blames her. The other one won't let go. Her name is Ruth.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `GO HOME TO YOUR MOTHERS.` → `ONE TURNS BACK. ONE WON'T.`

segments.voice: What Ruth says next, many people know by heart without knowing where it comes from. Most English speakers know it from the King James: "whither thou goest, I will go." The Douay-Rheims gives it like this: "whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go: and where thou shalt dwell, I also will dwell. Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." And she goes further: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. Notice who she's saying it to. Not a husband. A mother-in-law, old, grieving and broke, who has just told her to leave. Couples often read these words at weddings, and that's lovely. But first they were a daughter-in-law's vow to a widow with nothing to offer. The Hebrew storytellers have a word for what Ruth does: chesed, steady, loyal love that keeps showing up. Naomi even uses it on the road, praying that God will deal kindly with the two young women, as they have dealt with the dead and with her. Ruth is a foreigner, from Moab, a people Israel had old quarrels with. And she becomes, in this book, the picture of faithfulness. Then they reach Bethlehem, and the town women say, is this Naomi? And Naomi answers, in the Douay: "I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me back empty." Don't call me Naomi, she says, which means beautiful. Call me Mara, bitter. The book lets her say it. It doesn't correct her or rush her. It just keeps Ruth standing beside her, through the bitterness, at the start of the barley harvest.
screen: `WHITHER THOU GOEST, I WILL GO.` · `A VOW TO A MOTHER-IN-LAW.` · `CHESED — LOVE THAT STAYS.` · `CALL ME MARA, BITTER.` · then, large: `THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay with someone going through loss. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is grieving right now. A death, a divorce, a job, a diagnosis, a move they didn't want. Maybe, like Naomi, they've told everyone they're fine, or told everyone to go away. Picture yourself on the road beside them, not fixing anything, just walking. Ask what staying would look like this week. A message that doesn't need an answer. A meal. Sitting through the bitter part. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
Whither thou goest. Ruth's promise to Naomi, a vow of loyal love from a foreign daughter-in-law to a widow who had nothing left. Today's word.
Your line: thy people, my people. Today, reach out to one grieving person and stay a little longer than is comfortable. Day three hundred ninety-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: a romantic vow, read at weddings.
what it means: a young foreign widow refuses to leave her grieving mother-in-law, and binds her life, her people and her God to Naomi's.
what a scholar hears: chesed, loyal love, is a key word of the book. Naomi asks God to show it in 1:8, and Ruth lives it out on the road.

396.title: Gleaning (Ruth 2–4)
396.hook: Boaz leaves extra grain on purpose, and Ruth becomes David's great-grandmother
396.howItsDone: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and Catholic charities and parish food ministries often point to gleaning as a model of caring for the poor while protecting their dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth on the road to Bethlehem: whither thou goest, I will go. Your line was thy people, my people. Who did you stay with a little longer? Day three hundred ninety-six.

Two widows arrive in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest, and there's no food in the house. So Ruth does what the poor did in Israel. She goes out to a field behind the reapers and picks up what they drop. The law of Moses said farmers must not strip their fields bare: leave the edges, leave what falls, for the poor and the stranger. It was a safety net, built into the harvest. Ruth is both poor and a stranger. And the field she happens to walk into belongs to a man named Boaz, Booz in the Douay-Rheims, a relative of Naomi's dead husband. Today's word is what she does there all day.
screen: `NO FOOD IN THE HOUSE.` → `LEAVE THE EDGES FOR THE POOR.` → `A FIELD THAT BELONGS TO BOAZ.`

segments.voice: Gleaning means gathering what's left after the harvest: the stray ears of grain, the leftovers, the edges. It's slow, bent-over work, and it's the work of people with nothing else. Boaz walks out, sees the foreign woman, and asks who she is. He's already heard: everything she did for her mother-in-law has been told to him. So he protects her. Stay in my field, drink from my workers' water jars, eat with us at mealtime. Then, when she goes back to work, he quietly tells his young men this, in the Douay: "let fall some of your handfuls of purpose, and leave them, that she may gather them without shame." Of purpose. He doesn't hand her a sack of grain like a charity case. He arranges the field so her own work finds more, and her dignity stays whole. That evening she beats out what she gathered and has about an ephah of barley. In the chapters that follow, Naomi sends Ruth to Boaz at the threshing floor, and Boaz acts as the go'el, the kinsman who redeems a family's land and name. He marries Ruth. They have a son, Obed. And the book ends with a short family tree: Obed is the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David. A foreign widow who gathered leftovers becomes the great-grandmother of Israel's greatest king. Catholics hear one more step. When Matthew's Gospel opens with Jesus's family tree, Ruth is named in it, one of only a few women listed. Kindness on purpose, in one barley field, runs all the way to Bethlehem again.
screen: `GLEANING — GATHERING WHAT'S LEFT.` · `LET FALL SOME HANDFULS ON PURPOSE.` · `BOAZ, THE KINSMAN WHO REDEEMS.` · `GREAT-GRANDMOTHER OF DAVID.` · then, large: `THAT SHE MAY GATHER THEM WITHOUT SHAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave extra for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think about where your own field has edges. The extra in the grocery cart. The time after a meeting. The tip. The parking spot near the door. The credit for an idea. Pick one place where you could let something fall on purpose, so someone else can pick it up without feeling handed charity. Picture who that might be. Then picture doing it quietly, the way Boaz did, so nobody has to say thank you. If you pray, you can ask for eyes like his. The bell holds the time.
Gleaning. Gathering the grain left behind after harvest, which the law left for the poor and the stranger. Ruth gleaned in the field of Boaz. Today's word.
Your line: kindness on purpose. Today, leave one handful for someone, and don't tell them you did. Day three hundred ninety-six.

397.title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1–2)
397.hook: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk, then sings like Mary will
397.howItsDone: Catholics pray Hannah's song as one of the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours, at Morning Prayer, and many couples hoping for a child find company in her story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gleaning: Boaz telling his workers to drop grain on purpose for Ruth. Your line was kindness on purpose. What did you leave for someone? Day three hundred ninety-seven.

Every year a family travels up to the sanctuary at Shiloh, and every year it's the worst week of the year for one of them. Her name is Hannah, Anna in the Douay-Rheims. Her husband loves her, but she has no children, and his other wife has many, and that other wife needles her about it, year after year, until Hannah can't eat. Her husband tries to help: Am I not better to thee than ten children? It doesn't help. So one year, after the meal, she gets up, goes to the doorway of the house of the Lord, and starts to pray. An old priest named Eli is sitting there on a stool, watching.
screen: `THE YEARLY TRIP TO SHILOH.` → `NO CHILDREN, AND A RIVAL'S TAUNTS.` → `AN OLD PRIEST ON A STOOL, WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Hannah prays with tears. Her lips move, but no sound comes out. In those days people usually prayed aloud, so to Eli this looks like one thing: she's drunk. He tells her to go sleep it off. And she answers him, in the Douay: "I am an exceeding unhappy woman, and have drunk neither wine nor any strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the Lord." Poured out. Not a polite request. Everything in her, emptied out in front of God. And Eli, to his credit, changes his tune: go in peace, he says, and may God grant your petition. Then a small detail: after that, the text says, her face was no longer sad. Nothing has happened yet. She simply prayed and was heard. Then she has a son, Samuel, and when he's weaned she brings him back to Shiloh and gives him to the Lord's service, just as she vowed. And she sings. Her song begins: "My heart hath rejoiced in the Lord." And it turns the world upside down: the mighty are broken, the weak are girded with strength, the hungry are filled, and God lifts the poor from the dust to sit with princes. If that sounds familiar, it should. Centuries later, a young woman named Mary visits her cousin and sings: my soul doth magnify the Lord, he hath put down the mighty and exalted the humble, filled the hungry with good things. The Church has long heard Hannah's song as the older sister of Mary's Magnificat, and prays it among the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours.
screen: `LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` · `I HAVE POURED OUT MY SOUL.` · `HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.` · `A SONG THAT MARY WILL ECHO.` · then, large: `MY HEART HATH REJOICED IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pour out one honest prayer. Settle, and breathe. Think of the thing you've been carrying the longest, the ache you don't bring up anymore because people are tired of hearing it, or you are. Don't tidy it. If you pray, tell God exactly how it is, silently, the way Hannah did, lips moving if you like, with no polite words in front. If you don't pray, say it plainly to yourself, all of it, and let it be heard. Then just stay a moment, and notice your face. The bell holds the time.
Hannah's prayer. A silent, tearful prayer at Shiloh, so intense the priest thought she was drunk, and later a song of joy that Mary's Magnificat echoes. Today's word.
Your line: she poured out her soul. Today, when someone tells you something raw, believe them before you judge them, the way Eli finally did. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

398.title: Speak, Lord (1 Samuel 3)
398.hook: a boy wakes three times to a voice and learns to say speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth
398.howItsDone: Many Catholics use Samuel's words, speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth, as a short prayer before reading scripture or in quiet adoration, and the story is often read when the Church prays for vocations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah at Shiloh, praying so hard the priest thought she was drunk. Your line was she poured out her soul. Whose raw words did you believe? Today, the boy she prayed for. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

It's the middle of the night in the sanctuary at Shiloh. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. An old priest, Eli, is asleep in his place; his eyes have grown so dim he can barely see. And a boy is asleep near the ark of God. That's Samuel, Hannah's son, the one she gave to the Lord. The text adds a sad note about those days: the word of the Lord was rare, and visions were few. Then, in the dark, someone calls the boy's name. Samuel jumps up and runs to the old man. Here I am. You called me. Eli rolls over: I didn't call you. Go back to sleep.
screen: `NIGHT AT SHILOH.` → `THE WORD OF THE LORD WAS RARE.` → `HERE I AM. YOU CALLED ME.`

segments.voice: It happens again. Samuel runs to Eli, Eli sends him back. Then a third time. And the text gives the reason he keeps getting it wrong: "Samuel did not yet know the Lord." He's grown up in the house of God, he serves there every day, and he doesn't recognize God's voice. That's not a failure. It's just young. On the third time, the old man understands. Eli, who has his own failings, and whose sons have been a disgrace, still knows this much: it's God. So he gives the boy one line to say. In the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." Samuel goes back and lies down. And the text says the Lord came and stood, and called as before: Samuel, Samuel. And this time the boy says it. Notice what the line does. Speak comes first: Samuel asks for the word. Then heareth: he promises to listen. In Hebrew, the word for hearing is the same root as the Shema, the hear, O Israel this path met not long ago. Listening is the heart of it. And what God says is hard: judgment on Eli's house. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli insists, and Samuel tells him everything. Hearing God, it turns out, can mean carrying a message you'd rather not. The Church reads this chapter at Mass when it speaks about vocations, and for many Catholics, speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth is a whole prayer in itself. It needs no other words.
screen: `THREE TIMES TO THE WRONG ROOM.` · `SAMUEL DID NOT YET KNOW THE LORD.` · `THE OLD PRIEST GIVES HIM A LINE.` · `A HARD MESSAGE IN THE MORNING.` · then, large: `SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray those words and listen. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say Samuel's line once, slowly: Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth. Then stop talking. Don't fill the silence with requests. Just listen, the way you'd listen in a dark room for someone calling your name. If you don't pray, simply listen: to the room, to your breath, to whatever has been trying to get your attention lately. Nothing may come. That's all right. Samuel ran to the wrong room three times. The bell holds the time.
Speak. The first word of Samuel's answer in the night, and the start of a whole prayer: speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth. Today's word.
Your line: thy servant heareth. Today, in one conversation, listen all the way to the end before you answer. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 398 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SAUL, HEAD AND SHOULDERS TALLER.`

399.title: Saul, head and shoulders taller (1 Samuel 9–10)
399.hook: the first king is chosen, hiding among the baggage
399.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Saul's anointing in the weekday Mass readings, and the Church's own anointings, at baptism, confirmation and ordination with sacred chrism, carry on the old sign of oil poured on someone chosen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy in the night at Shiloh, learning to say speak, Lord. Your line was thy servant heareth. Who did you listen to all the way to the end? Day three hundred ninety-nine, the end of week fifty-seven.

A farmer's donkeys have wandered off. He sends his son and a servant to find them. They search the hill country for three days. Nothing. They're about to give up and go home when the servant says: there's a man of God in the next town. Maybe he can tell us where the donkeys went. So a tall young man walks into town looking for lost animals, and walks out a king. The man of God is Samuel, now grown old. The tall young man is Saul. The Bible says there was no goodlier person among the children of Israel, and that from his shoulders upward he stood above everyone.
screen: `THE LOST DONKEYS.` → `ASK THE MAN OF GOD.` → `LOOKING FOR ANIMALS, FOUND A CROWN.`

segments.voice: First, the backstory. Israel had asked Samuel for a king, to be like the nations around them, and the text treats that as a sad request: they're setting aside God as their king. God tells Samuel to give them one anyway. Then Samuel meets Saul, and before Saul can even ask about the donkeys, Samuel tells him: they're found, stop worrying. Then, privately, he takes a little vial of oil, pours it on Saul's head, and kisses him. The Lord has anointed you prince over his people. Anointed: in Hebrew, mashiach. It's the word that becomes Messiah, and in Greek, Christ. Here, at its start, it's simply oil on a nervous young man's head. And Saul is nervous. When Samuel first hints at greatness, Saul answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Am not I a son of Jemini of the least tribe of Israel?" Benjamin, the smallest tribe. Then comes the public choosing. All Israel gathers, lots are cast, tribe by tribe, family by family, and the lot falls on Saul. Everyone turns to look, and he isn't there. They ask the Lord where he is, and the answer comes, in the King James: "Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff." The baggage. The tallest man in Israel, crouched behind the luggage. They pull him out, he stands head and shoulders above them, and the people shout: "God save the king." It's a tender, almost funny beginning, and the story will darken: Saul's reign ends in jealousy and tragedy. But this week has been full of people who felt too small: Gideon in the winepress, Ruth the stranger, Hannah in tears, a boy in the dark. Saul makes one more.
screen: `ISRAEL ASKS FOR A KING.` · `OIL ON HIS HEAD: ANOINTED.` · `THE LEAST TRIBE OF ISRAEL.` · `HIDING AMONG THE STUFF.` · then, large: `GOD SAVE THE KING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice where you hide. Settle, and breathe. Saul hid behind the luggage at the exact moment he was called. Ask yourself where your luggage is. Busyness. Jokes. Your phone. Saying I'm not the right person. Letting someone louder go first. Don't judge it. Just notice one place you duck out of sight when you're being asked to stand up. Then picture stepping out, the way Saul finally did, and standing where people can see you. If you pray, you can ask for that courage. The bell holds the time.
Saul. Israel's first king, tall and frightened, anointed with oil by Samuel and found hiding among the baggage on the day he was chosen. Today's word.

Your line: hiding in the baggage. Today, step out once where you'd usually hide. And that's week fifty-seven: Gideon's fleece, Samson, Ruth on the road, gleaning, Hannah's prayer, speak, Lord, and Saul. Day three hundred ninety-nine.
